findings.interpretation_limits: Mediators and outcomes were not independently randomized; authors explicitly say cross-sectional serial pathway is not causal.

Appendix stimuli include technical claims that should not be treated as verified facts.

papers.title: The Language that Gets People to Give: Phrases that Predict Success on Kickstarter
papers.study_kind: observational predictive modeling with post-hoc qualitative interpretation
papers.scope: Kickstarter public crowdfunding pitches and rewards, 13 creative categories; pages scraped August 2012 after campaign end; funding outcome is goal achieved, not proposal merit or fulfillment.
papers.sample_and_design: 45,815 launched-project URLs, 45,810 retained after five non-ended; lasso logistic regression of 20,391 selected 1–3 grams plus 59 controls, ten-fold cross-validation and 80/20 train/test comparison. Homepages can change while campaign is live and include reward descriptions; controls include update counts, comments and Featured/Most Funded placement measured post hoc.
papers.outcomes: Binary funded versus not funded. No randomized wording intervention, reader understanding, funder decision mechanism or subsequent delivery outcome.

findings.claim: 23,604 of 45,810 campaigns funded (51.53%); 22,206 not funded (48.47%).
findings.interpretation_limits: US Kickstarter projects observed in 2012; not all proposal settings.

findings.claim: Reported cross-validation error was 17.03% controls-only versus 2.4% with phrases and controls (Table 2); Figure 3 reports 2.41% cross-validation and 2.24% held-out prediction error for alpha=1 using an 80/20 split.
findings.denominator: 45,810 campaign observations, ten-fold CV; split details not fully specified
findings.interpretation_limits: Retrospective homepage text and dynamic controls can include outcome information; neither evaluation establishes prospective launch-time performance. Figure 4 and adjacent prose do not clearly identify the metric basis.

findings.claim: Paper calls 58.56% a deviance drop/variance: given reported null, control and combined deviances 63,463.47, 37,525.52 and 363.42, the increment 37,162.10 divided by null deviance is 58.56%; relative to controls-only deviance it is about 99.03%.
findings.interpretation_limits: Not ordinary variance explained or a causal contribution; deviance from fitted models and wording internally inconsistent.

findings.claim: Positive and negative sentiment differences were reported statistically nonsignificant; the paper calls LIWC group differences small despite statistical significance.
findings.denominator: funded and unfunded campaign language groups; sample-level sentiment test denominator not separately stated
findings.interpretation_limits: Do not infer that positivity improves funding or no real effect exists.

limitations: Homepages were scraped after end and could have changed; page 10 shows live progress ("we’ve hit the 50% mark"). Updates, comments and Most Funded status are dynamic. Strong potential temporal leakage and reverse causation, not resolved by cross-validation.
No random assignment, no inference about individual phrases causing funding; category-wide filtering and Google presence do not establish transfer.

Paper describes the majority-class baseline as always choosing not-funded despite funded being the majority; 48.47% baseline error corresponds to predicting funded (pages 3 and 6). Figure 4 and adjacent prose do not clearly identify the metric basis; Figure 3 distinguishes cross-validation from held-out prediction error.
No independent prelaunch validation, calibration or selection-inside-fold audit established in supplied paper.
rule_implications: No lexical positive/negative phrase scoring, automatic assertiveness increase or funding guarantee. Clear, factual rewards and audience benefits may be worth presenting when true and relevant; reciprocity interpretation is an untested mechanism.
Reaffirm skills/write-with-purpose/references/concepts-and-claims.md: separate proposals, evidence, predictions and actual outcomes; preserve uncertainty.
data_or_code_leads: Paper page 11 lists historical KS.predicts and Gg.KS.pos/neg author URLs; access, version, data and rights not checked in this review. glmnet software is identified but no project code verified. No automatic GitHub adoption.
extraction_issues: Page 5 says 58.56% drop without clearly stating denominator; direct calculation shown above. Figure 3 distinguishes 2.41% cross-validation error from 2.24% held-out prediction error at alpha=1; Table 2 rounds cross-validation error to 2.4%. Figure 4 and adjacent prose are metric-ambiguous.
papers.practical_takeaway: Use proposal purposes and evidence, while separating retrospective prediction from an effect of changing wording.

findings.interpretation_limits: Style axis is PCA of a bundled manipulation; no individual component effect is isolated.

findings.claim: Understanding odds ratio 1.08 [1.01,1.15] per composite unit; p=.027, topic-adjusted mixed model.
findings.interpretation_limits: Two multiple-choice questions per abstract; odds ratio, not 8 percentage-point improvement.

findings.claim: Raw comprehension proportions nonmonotonic across easiest, easy, hard, hardest: 57.87%, 39.47%, 40.79%, 47.95%.
findings.denominator: 628 responses to understanding questions overall; per-level denominators not given
findings.interpretation_limits: Raw group proportions do not establish monotone dose-response; modeled result adjusts topic and reader.

findings.claim: No evidence of topic × difficulty or English-as-second-language effect in alternative models; authors caution sample not designed for ESL inference.
findings.interpretation_limits: Nonsignificance is not equivalence and subgroup sample is limited.

findings.claim: Table 2 reports easiest/hardest confidence 62.36%/48.78%; p.5 text instead gives 58.3%/44.1%, while discussion returns to 62%/49%.
findings.evidence_locator: Table 2 vs results prose and discussion
findings.denominator: 347 confidence responses; per-condition n not reported
findings.interpretation_limits: Unresolved internal discrepancy; avoid treating either contrast as independently verified.

limitations: Nine aspects vary together (including 0 hedges versus 4, acronyms, length, punctuation); isolated removal of any single feature is not tested.
Three created abstracts, student population, short testing and two questions limit domain and professional-reader generalization.
Results text and Table 2 differ on confidence means; Discussion p.6 inaccurately describes understanding as self-reported although methods explicitly describe multiple-choice scoring.
Authors retained content and logical flow by design, but whether all qualifications are equivalently represented is not independently audited.
papers.data_or_code_leads: Authors state raw data available on request p.7; supplementary abstract stimuli and alternative models linked in article. No code repository confirmed.
extraction_issues: Internal mismatch: Table 2 vs p.5 confidence means; retain both and no invented resolution.
Discussion p.6 calls all measures self-reported; methods and Tables 2–3 specify binary comprehension questions.
Table 3 confidence intercept appears extracted as 0.89 beside CI 66.30–75.47; not used.
papers.practical_takeaway: Compare bundled accessibility approaches while preserving necessary terms and uncertainty; individual ingredients were not isolated.

papers.title: Use of Promotional Language in Grant Applications and Grant Success
papers.study_kind: cross-sectional observational association study with regression and lexical validation
papers.scope: Biomedical grant applications to NNF in 2015–2022 and Northwestern faculty NIH submissions in 2007–2019; funded and rejected full application texts. Audience includes agency reviewers, not general workplace decision makers.
papers.sample_and_design: 9,096 NNF applications, 2,439 NIH applications from one university; dictionary fraction of 139 science-specific promotional words, logistic association with covariates including applicant performance and grant features and year/length fixed effects. Lexicon validation and five-fold cross-validation reported; released supplementary information and data statements not individually checked.
papers.outcomes: Binary funded/rejected and frequency of promotional terms; no randomized causal outcome, measured readability, merit or actual reviewer comprehension.

findings.claim: NNF awarded 1,579 of 9,096 applications (17.4%); NIH awarded 481 of 2,439 (19.7%).
findings.interpretation_limits: NIH cohort from one institution, NNF from one foundation; repeated applicants possible.

findings.claim: Adjusted odds ratios for promotional-word percentage were 1.47 (95% CI 1.25–1.71) NNF and 1.51 (1.10–2.11) NIH; methods indicate a one percentage-point increase in the fraction.
findings.denominator: 9,096 NNF and 2,439 NIH applications in full samples; exact model complete cases not stated in main text
findings.interpretation_limits: Odds ratios, not probability ratios or effects of editing. Figure 2 displays 1.46 for the NNF multivariable model; use prose 1.47 with rounding discrepancy flagged.

findings.claim: Mean dictionary-word fractions funded vs unfunded were 1.02% vs 0.98% for NNF and 0.93% vs 0.89% for NIH.
findings.interpretation_limits: Word fractions, not measures of inaccurate or unsupported hype; differences are descriptive.

findings.claim: NNF binscatter estimated 14% to 22% funding probability from lowest to highest promotional-language bin; paper also describes relative increase of 53%.
findings.denominator: 20 equal-size bins of NNF sample; exact bin counts not printed
findings.interpretation_limits: Approximate fitted sample association, not benefit from adding words; figure caption also calls 53% an odds increase, creating ambiguity.

findings.claim: Previous lexicon construction evaluated each candidate in at least 500 occurrences by two reviewers, with reported kappa 0.82.
findings.denominator: at least 500 contexts per candidate term, 139-term instrument
findings.interpretation_limits: Context-level agreement from earlier work; does not validate each token occurrence in every grant.

limitations: Observational covariate adjustment does not remove unmeasured project merit, reviewer expectations, selection or confounding; author notes need for causal studies (p8).
A dictionary term is not a judgment of exaggeration, truth or appropriateness in context. Their sample substitution examples are sometimes awkward or change intensity.
Five-fold validation reported (Fig 2) without predictive accuracy or independent temporal/external sample evaluation in main paper; does not establish causal or prospective performance.

Page 2 says 38.4% of NNF and 33.7% of NIH are women, with numerators using all applications although phrasing ambiguously follows awarded subset. Treat 3491/9096 and 823/2439 as full-application counts.
NIH sample and one private foundation do not represent other funders, disciplines or eras.
rule_implications: A blanket ban on adjectives or promotional lexemes conflicts with observed positive association, not proof of improved prose or reason to add adjectives.

Reaffirm evidence-backed positive emphasis and proposal significance when substantiated; retain uncertainty and voice. Flag ungrounded novelty, superlatives and promises for contextual review, never automatic deletion or insertion.
data_or_code_leads: Main paper pages 2, 9–10: NNF data obtainable through cooperative agreement on request; NIH data internal university request; supplement 1 lists dictionary, operationalization, model tables, supplement 2 data statement. Neither supplement inspected; no reproducible repository verified.
extraction_issues: Article uses causal wording ("can increase") but discussion explicitly calls for causal analyses; this review treats estimates as associations. NNF adjusted OR in main results 1.47 while figure 2 shows 1.46. Caption and text disagree about odds versus probability for 53% change.
papers.practical_takeaway: Allow truthful positive emphasis and check claims; promotional-word associations do not demonstrate a benefit from adding hype.

papers.title: The effect of writing style on success in grant applications
papers.study_kind: observational multivariable study of application language and review outcomes
papers.scope: One early-career funding scheme in 2014, disciplinary panels; project description, abstract and CV; funding selection has staged review, later presentation and peer review.
papers.sample_and_design: 3,207 applications received; 3,030 consented, 2,900 text-extractable after exclusions, 2,532 eligible following field and bibliometric exclusions; tables use 2,493 first-stage and 677 second-stage descriptions. English proficiency proxied by country-level score. LIWC 2015 English dictionaries; features standardized by panel; mixed, ordinal and logistic regressions control for panel, applicant publication impact and gender.
papers.outcomes: First and second-stage project scores, ordinal final score and decision to proceed/funding. Linguistic proxies are not observed comprehension or objective writing quality.

findings.claim: First-stage project-description model estimated certainty coefficient B=0.043 (95% CI 0.022–0.063; p<0.001); tentative words B=0.002 (95% CI −0.020–0.023; p=0.885).
findings.evidence_locator: Table 3, mixed model with panel fixed effects
findings.interpretation_limits: Coefficients panel-standardized, observational, no causal proof; a null result does not justify removing hedges.

findings.claim: First-stage progression model certainty OR 1.180 (95% CI 1.070–1.303); tentative OR 0.986 (0.890–1.093). Causal words OR 1.050 (0.952–1.158), not statistically significant.
findings.interpretation_limits: Per standardized predictor under model covariates; not final grant success. Do not add unsupported certainty or causal wording.

findings.claim: First-stage project score associations include positive word count B=0.501 and squared term B=−0.360, and positive words/sentence B=0.135 with squared B=−0.159.
findings.interpretation_limits: Joint quadratic model, panel-standardized; do not turn into a target or claim that increasing length causes success.

findings.claim: In stage two, project score model common words B=−0.030, p=0.036; final funding model common words OR=0.863, 95% CI 0.707–1.053, p=0.146.
findings.interpretation_limits: Different outcomes; later-stage sample selected on earlier success. Paper overgeneralizes significance to both outcomes.

findings.claim: For final ordinal score model, Nagelkerke pseudo-R² was 0.191 for full model and 0.146 linguistic-only; first-stage progression 0.131 and 0.100 respectively.
findings.interpretation_limits: Pseudo-R² is model fit statistic, not ordinary variance explained or out-of-sample accuracy; no external model validation is reported.

findings.claim: Abstract model shows tentative words B=0.024, p=0.025 for stage-one project score; most other abstract associations were not statistically significant.
findings.interpretation_limits: Paper’s blanket conclusion of no abstract effects overstates its own table; exploratory multiple comparisons and proxy interpretation cautions.

limitations: Single year, one scheme, early career and pre-set section/page constraints. Excluded humanities, law and qualitative social sciences and applicants missing bibliometric records.

Country nationality-based English score is crude; LIWC common-word frequency conflates technical content with readability; LIWC analytic score is not demonstrated narrative quality; measures do not establish mechanisms.
Selection into second stage, intervening extended applications and oral panel presentation confound comparisons across stages.
No held-out prospective predictive assessment or causal intervention reported; significance is not measured effect of an edit.
Table 9 duplicates first-stage decision coefficients in last column, and Table 3 extracted confidence intervals have apparent inconsistencies; verify typeset table before reuse.
rule_implications: Refine plain-language suggestions to preserve necessary technical content and vary syntax for reader function; do not impose short sentences, simple words or a complexity target.
Reaffirm preserving uncertainty; tentative terms not shown harmful, and may be epistemically necessary; candidate reassurance cannot raise modality.
Use section and audience context when reviewing presentation rather than translating LIWC narrative and analytic indexes into paragraph-function labels.
data_or_code_leads: LIWC 2015 identified as third-party software, not a demonstrated open corpus or codebook; applications collected under consent and no reusable release verified.
extraction_issues: Paper uses effect/causal language despite observational design. Narrative interpretations are proxies; Table 10 conflicts with blanket abstract null conclusion, Table 7 with blanket stage-two common-words statement.
papers.practical_takeaway: Respect section, stage and nonlinear variation; no transferable word/sentence target or universal penalty on tentative words.

papers.title: Style, content, and the success of ideas
papers.study_kind: Observational predictive analyses plus randomized one-sentence experiments
papers.scope: Five social science fields from selected JSTOR journals, plus online volunteer ratings of isolated research descriptions; citations or perceived importance/impact, not measured actual learning.
papers.sample_and_design: 28,774 research articles, 1990–2018; nine LIWC function-word category rates as style features, LDA topic mixture as content proxies, journal/year and other controls; negative-binomial and neural-network models. Exploratory section-level analyses. MTurk personal voice experiment N=185 and Prolific tense experiment N=234.
papers.outcomes: Google Scholar citation counts observationally; randomized experiments 1–7 perceived importance and expected impact, not actual citations.

findings.claim: Adding style features adjusted R² .208 to .217 in negative-binomial model; neural model predicted R² .209 to .234. Authors express gains as 4–11% of model-explained variance, not 4–11% of all variance.
findings.interpretation_limits: Topic controls and function words are proxies, not clean separation of all content and style; model comparison is predictive, not causal.

findings.claim: Exploratory first-person coefficients: front end b=.076 p<.001; empirical middle b=−.029 p=.016; conclusion b=.007 p=.29.
findings.denominator: Article corpus; section analysis, exact eligible denominator not explicitly given in text
findings.interpretation_limits: Adjusted negative-binomial coefficients, not percentage citation change; section classification and confounding remain.

findings.claim: Article/preposition coefficients front −.034/−.015; middle −.002 (p=.66)/+.027 (p<.001).
findings.denominator: Article corpus; exact section denominator not stated
findings.interpretation_limits: Preposition and article frequency is not comprehension; direction varies by section; p for middle article is nonsignificant.

findings.claim: Personal-voice randomized condition vs control: importance 6.15 vs 5.76 and expected impact 5.97 vs 5.39, on 1–7 scales.
findings.interpretation_limits: One sentence, perceived outcomes, not citation or comprehension; treatment changes subject framing.

findings.claim: Present vs past condition: importance 5.97 vs 5.60 and expected impact 5.69 vs 5.20, on 1–7 scales.
findings.denominator: 234 Prolific participants per Method; reported impact F(1,200) has inconsistent denominator
findings.interpretation_limits: One sentence; changes tense/aspect and perceived currentness, potentially factual meaning. Printed mediation paragraph incorrectly names personal voice.

limitations: Function words carry grammatical and semantic meaning: pronouns change attribution and agency, tense/aspect changes temporal state, prepositions and negation scope. Topic mixture cannot isolate content quality or novelty; authors acknowledge this p.11.
Journal fixed effects and many controls reduce some confounding but do not remove unobserved topic quality, authorship or selection.
Section-level analyses are exploratory and paper reports null interactions; coefficients do not justify uniform first person or removal of articles/prepositions.
Study 3 and 4 manipulate a single vignette each and measure perceptions. Causal effect is for text versions and stated ratings only; mediators observational.
data_or_code_leads: Paper references supplementary S1–S9 and LIWC dictionaries, JSTOR source and Publish or Perish; full datasets and permissions are not established by this review.
extraction_issues: p.10 Study 4 uses personal voice in mediation paragraph despite a tense manipulation; reported F(1,200) for impact differs from N=234 and importance F(1,232). Preserve discrepancy rather than silently fixing.
papers.practical_takeaway: Consider voice and connecting language in context; small predictive improvements and sentence judgments do not establish whole-piece impact.

papers.title: Negativity drives online news consumption
papers.study_kind: Registered report; multilevel analysis of randomized field headline/package experiments
papers.scope: Upworthy English viral-news headline previews, 2013–2015; aggregate CTR.
papers.sample_and_design: Confirmatory release: 22,743 experiments before filtering; exclude single headline tests, combine duplicate headlines including across images; 12,448 remaining experiments. Binomial model random intercepts and varying slopes with length, fog index, positive/negative lexical scores, time. Whole variants randomized; emotion tokens are post hoc attributes, not randomized word interventions. Archive aggregates headline impressions and clicks, not individual users; independence across experiments asserted by authors but repeated users cannot be tested.
outcomes: clicks per impression; no direct measurement of sentiment, comprehension, satisfaction, share or writing quality

findings.claim: After filtering: 12,448 experiments, 53,699 headline variations, more than 205 million impressions and 2,778,124 clicks; mean 4.31 variants per experiment.
findings.interpretation_limits: Figure 2 caption reports 53,669, whereas text and Table 3 report 53,699.

findings.claim: Negative score β=0.015, 99% CI 0.013–0.018 per standardized proportion; authors estimate 2.3% relative CTR increase for each additional negative word at average 14.965-word headline.
findings.evidence_locator: Effect of negative language; model standardization
findings.interpretation_limits: Not 2.3 percentage points; model estimate rather than randomized isolated-word substitution; lexical choices and other wording may change together.

findings.claim: Positive score β=−0.008 (99% CI −0.010 to −0.006); authors estimate 1.0% relative CTR decrease per positive word for mean-length headline.
findings.interpretation_limits: P07 found no support for its positive-word hypothesis; different selection, estimands, modeling and lexicon processing on overlapping archive.

findings.claim: Secondary discrete-emotion scores: sadness β=0.006; fear β=−0.007; joy β=−0.009; anger β≈0, p=0.666 and equivalence test inconclusive.
findings.denominator: same filtered corpus, modeled dictionary emotion proportions
findings.interpretation_limits: Fear sign opposes preregistered hypothesis; non-significant anger does not establish no effect. Different outcome from sharing; emotion label is lexical proxy.

findings.claim: Varying-slope model: negative β=0.018 (99% CI 0.011–0.025), positive β=−0.017 (−0.023 to −0.010).
findings.interpretation_limits: Associations under model; image variation could co-occur though authors report robustness excluding image RCTs.

limitations: Samples share Upworthy archive with P04 and P07; overlap size not established. Do not count as independent replications.

Same story randomized variants identify effects of packages; lexical feature coefficients are observational post-treatment classifications with possible residual wording/image confounding, despite author causal language.
Dictionary and negation heuristics do not directly measure experienced emotion; same-user exposure or demographics not available.
p4 Fig 2 caption 53,669 conflicts with Table 3 and p3 53,699; p4 complexity prose prints +0.004 with negative z and interval.
data_or_code_leads: https://osf.io/uscpf/ (paper-reported data and analysis code; not independently audited)
https://www.liwc.app/ (paper says commercial purchase; no redistribution implied)
https://nrc.canada.ca/en/research-development/products-services/technical-advisory-services/sentiment-emotion-lexicons (public download, license not verified)
extraction_issues: Figure 2 caption denominator conflicts with paper text/table; complexity coefficient sign typo conflicts with z and interval.
papers.practical_takeaway: Keep negativity/attention optional and purpose-bound; whole headline packages were randomized, individual word effects are model-dependent.

papers.title: Ten Simple (Empirical) Rules for Writing Science
papers.study_kind: Editorial containing an observational quantitative analysis of article-abstract features and citations; not a systematic review, intervention trial or causal test
papers.scope: All six supplied main-paper pages and all five pages of official S1 Supporting Information reviewed. Abstracts from scientific articles rather than full-text professional writing.
papers.sample_and_design: Scopus records marked Article, published 1996–2012 and downloaded May 2013 in eight JCR categories. Excluded abstracts under 50 words, records with no author or fewer than 10 references; 1,065,139 category records remained. Some journals belong to multiple categories, so records need not represent independent articles (S1 pp. 1–2). Separate linear regressions by discipline and abstract feature and then journal; outcome log(citations+1), journal-year categorical effects, journal-standardized author count, reference count and feature (S1 pp. 2–3).
outcomes: Total citations as proxy for author-defined success, not comprehension, writing quality, causal influence or reader preference

findings.claim: Rule-proxy associations and direction are inventoried individually in rule_tests.
findings.denominator: More than one million abstracts across eight selected disciplines and 17 years; individual cell denominators in inaccessible supplement
findings.interpretation_limits: Citation is observational and proxies imperfect; significance sign is not effect size; heterogeneity and multiple comparisons apply.

findings.claim: Figure 1 uses 0.01/15 as per-feature criterion, Bonferroni adjustment toward an overall 1% level.
findings.interpretation_limits: Do not infer unreported precise p-values or correct for additional tests not described in supplied main text.

findings.claim: Authors give example one-standard-deviation journal-relative changes of +4.6% for a mathematics novelty measure and −7.2% for a geology shorter-abstract measure.
findings.denominator: One SD of stated feature relative to journal; mathematical scale and full model details depend on S1 Text
findings.interpretation_limits: These are model associations, not causal impacts; the prose and features require direction-aware interpretation.

findings.claim: Authors report sign changes in three of fifteen measured features across fields.
findings.denominator: 15 abstract feature proxies across eight disciplines
findings.interpretation_limits: A sign-change summary is not evidence of equal magnitude, non-significance, or no important within-discipline variation.

findings.claim: May 2013 Scopus category sample retained 1,065,139 records after excluding abstracts under 50 words, missing author, or fewer than ten references; articles span 1996–2012.
findings.denominator: 1,065,139 retained category records, not necessarily unique articles; 8 categories with overlapping journals
findings.interpretation_limits: Selection filters exclude short abstracts and sparsely referenced articles; Scopus Article indexing is selection by database classification, not independently verified original-research status.

findings.claim: Each feature was fitted separately in linear regressions on log(citations+1), with journal-year indicators and within-journal standardized numbers of authors and references; feature standardization is over all years in the journal.
findings.denominator: Separate category-by-feature regressions and journal-level analyses
findings.interpretation_limits: Coefficients do not jointly adjust for other correlated writing features. The exp(coefficient) ratio is exact for predicted citations+1 on the model scale, not exact for citations alone; no causal interpretation.

findings.claim: Keyword feature is unavailable when keywords are not reported; affect scores set out-of-dictionary words to zero; tense proxy also includes gerunds and past participles.
findings.evidence_locator: S1 Abstract Features R4, R6, R10
findings.denominator: R6 analyses restricted by keyword availability; feature-specific usable counts not specified in supplement
findings.interpretation_limits: Missingness may alter R6 analysis population. NLP tagging and dictionary proxy quality or zero denominator handling are not evaluated in supplied supplement.

rule_tests.reported_direction: Fewer words and fewer sentences associated with fewer citations across disciplines
rule_tests.interpretation_limit: Journal limits or readers may require brevity; longer text may add necessary detail or noise.
rule_tests.denominator: 1,065,139 retained category records overall; per-feature and discipline-specific eligible counts vary and are not supplied; categories can overlap
rule_tests.evidence_locator: Rule descriptions pp. 1–3 and Results/Fig. 1 p. 3

rule_tests.operational_proxy: sentence length relative to journal mean
rule_tests.reported_direction: Short sentences associated with citation benefit only in mathematics and physics
rule_tests.interpretation_limit: Sentence length is not a direct test of comprehensibility, cohesion or syntactic complexity.
rule_tests.denominator: 1,065,139 retained category records overall; per-feature and discipline-specific eligible counts vary and are not supplied; categories can overlap
rule_tests.evidence_locator: Rule descriptions pp. 1–3 and Results/Fig. 1 p. 3

rule_tests.operational_proxy: Share of unique words appearing in GNU Aspell or 2,954-word Dale–Chall list (S1 p. 3)
rule_tests.reported_direction: Fewer common/easy words associated with more citations
rule_tests.interpretation_limit: Dictionary membership is a poor proxy for jargon or audience understanding; retain necessary terminology.
rule_tests.denominator: 1,065,139 retained category records overall; per-feature and discipline-specific eligible counts vary and are not supplied; categories can overlap
rule_tests.evidence_locator: Rule descriptions pp. 1–3 and Results/Fig. 1 p. 3

rule_tests.operational_proxy: (present + gerund)/(present + gerund + past + past participle), NLTK tagged (S1 p. 3)
rule_tests.reported_direction: Positive association in biology and psychology, negative in chemistry and physics
rule_tests.interpretation_limit: Tense must reflect chronology and study status; association does not establish readability.
rule_tests.denominator: 1,065,139 retained category records overall; per-feature and discipline-specific eligible counts vary and are not supplied; categories can overlap
rule_tests.evidence_locator: Rule descriptions pp. 1–3 and Results/Fig. 1 p. 3

rule_tests.reported_direction: More modifiers associated with more citations
rule_tests.interpretation_limit: No inference that modifiers improve prose or that indiscriminate adjectives help.
rule_tests.denominator: 1,065,139 retained category records overall; per-feature and discipline-specific eligible counts vary and are not supplied; categories can overlap
rule_tests.evidence_locator: Rule descriptions pp. 1–3 and Results/Fig. 1 p. 3

rule_tests.operational_proxy: Count of abstract words matching keywords; unavailable when no keywords are reported (S1 p. 4)
rule_tests.reported_direction: Greater keyword matching associated with fewer citations
rule_tests.interpretation_limit: Keyword overlap is a weak proxy for conceptual focus; no automatic keyword avoidance.
rule_tests.denominator: 1,065,139 retained category records overall; per-feature and discipline-specific eligible counts vary and are not supplied; categories can overlap
rule_tests.evidence_locator: Rule descriptions pp. 1–3 and Results/Fig. 1 p. 3

rule_tests.operational_proxy: presence of novelty or importance marker words
rule_tests.interpretation_limit: A marker is neither actual novelty nor justified significance; avoid fabricated superlatives.
rule_tests.denominator: 1,065,139 retained category records overall; per-feature and discipline-specific eligible counts vary and are not supplied; categories can overlap
rule_tests.evidence_locator: Rule descriptions pp. 1–3 and Results/Fig. 1 p. 3

rule_tests.reported_direction: Greater superlative ratio associated with more citations
rule_tests.interpretation_limit: The feature does not test accurate confidence, causal quality or reader trust.
rule_tests.denominator: 1,065,139 retained category records overall; per-feature and discipline-specific eligible counts vary and are not supplied; categories can overlap
rule_tests.evidence_locator: Rule descriptions pp. 1–3 and Results/Fig. 1 p. 3

rule_tests.reported_direction: Fewer hedge words associated negatively in biology and physics, positively in chemistry
rule_tests.interpretation_limit: Study does not measure calibration: uncertainty and qualification may be required.
rule_tests.denominator: 1,065,139 retained category records overall; per-feature and discipline-specific eligible counts vary and are not supplied; categories can overlap
rule_tests.evidence_locator: Rule descriptions pp. 1–3 and Results/Fig. 1 p. 3

rule_tests.operational_proxy: Whissell affect dictionary values summed per word, unmatched words zero, divided by abstract words (S1 p. 4)
rule_tests.reported_direction: Higher affect-word dimensions associated with more citations
rule_tests.interpretation_limit: Lexicon is an affect proxy, not a measure of helpful metaphor or voice.
rule_tests.denominator: 1,065,139 retained category records overall; per-feature and discipline-specific eligible counts vary and are not supplied; categories can overlap
rule_tests.evidence_locator: Rule descriptions pp. 1–3 and Results/Fig. 1 p. 3

limitations: Observational citation associations can reflect journal selection, research content/quality, topic, exposure and other unmeasured confounding; author’s retrievability mechanism is an untested hypothesis (p. 4).
A dictionary match or keyword count is a proxy, not observed comprehension, focus or human judgment; comparison of features to citations does not validate any general stylistic instruction.
Abstracts have journal-enforced length and format constraints and are not full documents, paragraph functions or all writing.

S1 confirms that each feature was modeled separately; correlated features may confound each other. Journal-year indicators and author/reference counts do not remove topic, study-quality, exposure, or selection confounding (S1 pp. 2–3).

The model uses log(citations+1): exponentiated coefficient measures the modeled ratio of citations+1; the stated percentage change in citations is approximate and especially uncertain near zero (S1 p. 3). Main text and supplement give significance thresholds and example estimates but do not supply individual confidence intervals or fully inspectable model results in extracted supplement.

Scopus Article selection, minimum 50-word abstract and minimum 10 references constrain generalization. Overlapping journal categories prevent treating counts as independent disciplines or unique articles (S1 pp. 1–2).

Keywords missing are set to not available; excluded count and treatment in regression are not detailed. Tagger and dictionary errors and zero denominator cases are not assessed in the provided text (S1 pp. 3–4).
data_or_code_leads: PLOS supporting methods S1 retrieved and read: https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article/file?type=supplementary&id=info:doi/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1004205.s001 . Official receipt: experiments/evidence-integration-2026-11-16/supplement-attempts.json; prior web-tool signed redirect failed before successful direct publisher retrieval.
Authors used R biglm and NLTK; no raw Scopus data, project code repository or text rights confirmed. Main article is CC BY (p. 1), which does not license Scopus records.
extraction_issues: Main article Figure 1/2 image data are not fully represented by plain text. Supplement pp. 4–5 reference per-journal graphs without reproducing numeric coefficients in extracted text.
Supplement p. 3 calls dictionary proportions R2a/R2b despite main text labeling R3a/R3b; interpret as the R3 prose descriptions, preserving discrepancy.
Initial web-tool supplement fetch failed; the parent subsequently retrieved the verified official publisher PDF through direct endpoint. No raw Scopus corpus or independent replication.
papers.practical_takeaway: Question familiar style maxims; one-feature citation models are not causal writing advice or a universal inverse recipe.

papers.title: Generic structure and rhetorical moves in English-language empirical law research articles: Sites of interdisciplinary and interdiscursive cross-over
papers.scope: Empirical socio-legal research articles for scholarly readership, 2010–2012, three selected English-language journals; not theoretical legal essays, court decisions, or policy proposals.
papers.sample_and_design: 90 randomly selected Article-category papers, 30 per journal and 10 per journal-year; 1,079,527 tokens excluding footnotes and references. Manual functional-semantic analysis of headings, clause/sentence moves and frequencies. Selection restricts journal and article type (PDF p. 3 Tables 1–2, p. 4).
papers.outcomes: Section heading categories, rhetorical macro-organization, move and step frequencies, and selected lexical realizations; no reader experiment or writing-quality causal outcome.

Abstract: Setting the background for the study and its importance
Mentioning gaps addressed by the study
Stating the purpose, question, hypothesis of study
Stating the findings (qualitative or quantitative) or argument
Results: Restating data collection and analysis procedure

9: Announcing present research descriptively and/or purposively
12: Defining and developing methods, theories, concepts, issues, phenomena
Presenting the value of the study
15: Describing measures of variability for significant difference

findings.claim: Background review present in 79, absent in 11.
findings.interpretation_limit: Presence does not mandate a separate section; heading genres vary.

findings.claim: 75 independent Conclusion sections, and seven Discussion/Conclusion or Discussion/Implications blends; 82 total independent plus blended conclusions.
findings.interpretation_limit: Section-level pattern, not a paragraph function quota.

findings.claim: 12 blended-section occurrences: 1 Methods/Results, 4 Results/Discussion and 7 Discussion/Conclusion.
findings.denominator: 90 articles; 12 occurrences, not verified as 12 distinct documents
findings.interpretation_limit: Blending may coexist with separate analytical units.

findings.claim: 25 moves, with 6/3/3/3/3/4/3 per Abstract/Introduction/Background Review/Method/Results/Discussion/Conclusion; recursively patterned in every section and occasionally inverted.
findings.denominator: 90 selected articles; the claim every section is author statement

findings.claim: Abstract moves purpose, methodology, findings, conclusion each 100%; background 44%, gap 28%.
findings.interpretation_limit: Step percentages are ambiguous in denominator: avoid converting to counts.

findings.claim: Author reports 100% inter-rater agreement with one other applied-linguistics author.
findings.denominator: Coding sample size, independent/consensus protocol and metric not specified
findings.interpretation_limit: Do not compare directly to our exact-set agreement.

limitations: Table 3 says 33 unlabelled introductions but prints 27%; 33/90 is 36.7%. Its Results heading subtotals 65+10+15=90 despite underlying journal rows summing to more than 90; do not silently repair.
Step percentages generally sum to 100 within a move but denominator is not clearly stated; do not convert them into article prevalence.
Authors use obligatory for 100% observed corpus moves; sample and coding not a universal requirement.
Supplementary list of article identities mentioned PDF p.3 footnote; annotated corpus release not verified.
data_or_code_leads: PDF p.3 footnote says full sampled article list is in supplementary materials; actual files and terms unverified.
extraction_issues: Table 3 contains arithmetic inconsistencies as printed; Table 5 multiline rows retain blank 16A frequency.
papers.practical_takeaway: Preserve empirical-law section variation, blending and recursive moves; heading does not uniquely identify purpose.

papers.title: In search of commonalities: Some linguistic and rhetorical features of business reports as a genre
papers.study_kind: primarily qualitative descriptive genre corpus study
papers.scope: Authentic internal and external business reports, mainly Hong Kong with Singapore, Malaysia and UK sources, prepared for organizational clients, management, stakeholders or public; not a sample of decision memos per se.
papers.sample_and_design: 22 nonrandom convenience samples submitted by organizations; 12 external and 10 internal, 7 review, 6 problem-solving, 5 market and 4 feasibility reports. Management authors and some collective authorship; writers interviewed where possible, exact interview count not given (PDF pp. 4–6).
papers.outcomes: Observed macro organization, recommendations, rhetorical patterns and lexico-grammar; not independent measurement of decision outcomes or reader comprehension.

macro_options: topical sections containing findings and interpretations/conclusions

papers.step_inventory: Finding, interpretation and recommendation can occur in varying order and recur by topic; Toulmin roles are analytical relations, not mandatory paragraph sequence (PDF pp. 10, 14).

findings.claim: 19 reports contain clearly stated recommendations, and seven have clear recommendation headings; elsewhere paper says only two reports lack explicit recommendations.
findings.interpretation_limit: 19+2 does not account for all 22 under apparently similar wording; unresolved rather than silently reconciled.

findings.claim: Four conclusion sections, all summaries of recommendations; one report used the described conventional heading pattern.
findings.interpretation_limit: Predominantly qualitative, small heterogeneous convenience sample.

findings.claim: Report lengths range 409–28,593 words, median 4,614.
findings.interpretation_limit: Historical descriptive range only, not a target or minimum/maximum.

findings.claim: One full-length feasibility report has a separate clearly labelled methods section; methods otherwise often brief or absent.
findings.interpretation_limit: Paper says no examples of extensive appendical methods in corpus; brief reporting is not evidence that omitting methods is safe.

findings.claim: The suggested data/interpretation/recommendation sequence can vary; warrants may be implicit or explicit.
findings.denominator: Qualitative across corpus; no exact count for the cycle
findings.interpretation_limit: Do not force three moves or infer implicit support without contextual judgment.

limitations: Organizations supplied examples, not random or representative; mostly Hong Kong and medium/large firms. Paper stresses its qualitative size limitation and seeks quantitative replication (pp. 5, 22–23).
19/22 vs only two without explicit recommendation wording is unresolved.
No coder agreement method or downloadable coded dataset identified in full text; example business figures anonymized.
The author claims an inherent implicit recommendation even for sales reports; inference, not a directly observed reader action.
data_or_code_leads: No open coded data or codebook release identified in paper; quotations contain confidential anonymization.
extraction_issues: Observed numbers 19 with clearly stated recommendations and two without explicit recommendations are textually inconsistent; preserve as reported.
papers.practical_takeaway: Expose findings, interpretation, warrant and recommendation when the decision requires them; retain diverse report structures.

papers.title: A move/step model for methods sections: Demonstrating Rigour and Credibility
papers.study_kind: multidisciplinary descriptive corpus and expert-consultation study
papers.scope: Methods sections of IMRD experimental research articles; excludes disciplines whose scholarship differs substantially, such as mathematics, statistics, architecture and history (PDF p. 4).
papers.sample_and_design: 900 texts in 30 disciplines, 30 selected articles per discipline from 3–5 reputable journals; 150 exemplary sections seeded coding; expert-selected recent studies and one consultant per discipline limit representativeness; 1,423,131 words. Human annotations with sentence/phrase units and secondary overlapping functions (PDF pp. 3–6).
papers.outcomes: Functional-semantic move/step inventories and annotated unit frequency, sequences, consultant perceived occurrence, discipline clustering. No direct test of improved writing outcomes.
papers.step_inventory: Six, seven and three steps, respectively; see move_inventory counts and names. Numbering is not a prescribed order. Table 3 labels counts as sentences, while surrounding text calls overall counts functional units; sentence/phrase overlaps preclude treating these as independently observed document prevalence (PDF pp. 6, 8, 10, 12).

findings.claim: Three annotators: ICC .86 for moves and .80 for steps, using a two-way mixed-effects model, calculated throughout.
findings.denominator: three annotators; number and sampling of doubly/triply coded units unspecified
findings.interpretation_limit: ICC is not our paragraph exact-set agreement; no metric equivalence or accuracy claim.

findings.claim: 94,925 annotated functional units: 21,397 Move 1 (22%), 67,337 Move 2 (71%), 6,191 Move 3 (7%).
findings.interpretation_limit: Paper describes Move 1 as optional based on distribution but also says all 900 texts contain it; unit share is not document prevalence.

findings.claim: All 16 steps observed overall; Table 3 lists within-move sentence counts including Move 2 tools 30,693/67,337 = 45.6%.
findings.denominator: move-specific counts; table labels them sentences and allows overlapping functional tags
findings.interpretation_limit: No claim that 45.6% of documents have this step or should allocate that much space.

findings.claim: All seven Move 2 steps occur in each of 30 disciplines at aggregate level; Move 3 absent from some individual texts.
findings.interpretation_limit: Discipline-level presence does not imply occurrence in each paper.

findings.claim: Reporting incrementals identified in all 30 disciplines; experts report it as rare 40% or lacking 8%.
findings.denominator: 30 disciplines for corpus; consultant response denominator not explicitly clear from extracted text
findings.interpretation_limit: Expert judgments and corpus measurements have different units; interpret contrast, not exact contradiction.

findings.claim: Step transition likelihoods computed on the larger related IMRD corpus; reported zero transitions are sample/model observations.
findings.denominator: Related larger corpus includes Methods sample, so not independent replication
findings.interpretation_limit: Do not forbid zero-probability transitions in new writing.

limitations: One faculty consultant per discipline, purposively selected 30 studies per field, and explicitly excluded non-IMRD disciplinary traditions; no representative prevalence claim.
Paper does not perform full lexico-grammatical realization analysis (PDF p.16).
Unit share vs document presence conflated in author’s optionality label; do not adopt.
One source paragraph misnames Move 2 Step 7 as rationalizing, whereas inventory and definition show Step 6 rationalizing and Step 7 reporting incrementals (PDF pp.9,15).
Original study imposes primary label and secondary label; this project does not require a primary function.
data_or_code_leads: Authors report annotated corpus used through Callisto or other platforms and a move/step functional concordancer (PDF pp.15–16); release URL, data rights, model and corpus files remain unverified.
extraction_issues: Table 3 labels step frequencies sentences; paper elsewhere calls totals functional segments. Report denominator as printed and preserve overlap.
papers.practical_takeaway: Seed Methods questions from three moves and sixteen steps; do not impose sequence, step quotas or cross-form templates.

papers.title: Interrater agreement in genre analysis: A methodological review and a comparison of three measures
papers.study_kind: Systematic methodological review plus observational methodological comparison of agreement metrics, not meta-analysis or randomized trial
papers.scope: EAP research article move-step studies; social-science article introductions for direct coding; printed pages match PDF pages. All supplied text pp. 1–17 reviewed including appendices and references.
papers.sample_and_design: LLBA and Google Scholar returned 341 and 1,430 records, respectively; peer-reviewed manual research-article move analyses only, 2003–January 2023; 65 included. Three experienced doctoral researchers coded 65 review studies independently after instrument development (16 fields), then reconciled. Separately, nine introductions (258 sentence units) were used for practice and 26 introductions (908 sentence units) for metric comparison; all 35 from COSSRAI, not 35 in evaluation (pp. 6–7).
outcomes: Percent agreement, Cohen/Fleiss kappa, multi-valued alpha and benchmarking with Gwet AC1
No direct semantic ground truth, writing quality or reader comprehension measurement

findings.claim: Review reporting gaps: 38 studies did not report agreement; nine mentioned multifunctionality, and six of those discussed handling it.
findings.interpretation_limits: Non-reporting does not prove the procedure was not done; review excludes automatic/semi-automatic studies.

findings.claim: Review-code instrument has 16 fields in five categories; reviewers report average 95.38% agreement, Fleiss kappa 0.94 and alpha 0.94.
findings.denominator: Three independent coders of 65 papers; average across review-code items
findings.interpretation_limits: These describe coding the literature review, not reliability of rhetorical labels; averaging method is not fully specified in main text.

findings.claim: Rhetorical chunk is analytic concept but every affected sentence is a fixed annotation unit; repeated functions extend to each sentence and different within-sentence clauses can yield multiple tags.
findings.denominator: 26 introductions, 908 sentence units after nine training texts
findings.interpretation_limits: Fixed sentence assignment does not establish independent boundary agreement or actual sub-sentence realization spans.

findings.claim: Among 908 sentence units, 236 had multiple tags from at least one rater; authors state 671 were monofunctional throughout.
findings.interpretation_limits: 236 + 671 = 907, not 908; the text does not explain the remaining unit. Do not silently treat it as missing or infer missingness.

findings.claim: Agreement falls as categories increase from 3 move labels to 14 broad steps and 22 fine steps; one coder pair has higher multivalue alpha than single-label kappa because order of primary/secondary functions differs.
findings.interpretation_limits: Graph values not extracted; pair-dependent results do not establish accuracy or general superiority.

findings.claim: For this sample, authors report AC1 and kappa differences around 2% after curves level at 750 units and suggest larger samples and more than two raters.
findings.denominator: 908 sentence units, three raters; recommendation cites approximately 750 units or 22 texts
findings.interpretation_limits: This is a sample-specific descriptive finding, not a transferable minimum or a guarantee of stability; ordering/clustering by article matters.

findings.claim: For review papers, Fig. 3 reports 27 of 65 studies report an agreement type while prose says 28 clearly report results.
findings.interpretation_limits: Reporting definitions or source accounting may differ; discrepancy unresolved.

limitations: Metric comparison uses same three trained human genre researchers and selected social science introductions; sensitivity to rater pairing, label prevalence and granularity limits transfer.

Nominal multi-valued disagreement uses 1 − 2|C∩K|/(|C|+|K|), with both empty sets treated as zero disagreement (p. 5 Table 1); alpha corrects observed disagreement against expected disagreement. Set order is ignored. Empty versus unassessed/missing must not be conflated.
Paper discusses fixed units rather than independently locating realization boundaries; no justification that sentence coding captures the exact extent or target of every rhetorical function.

Article does not report missing-item handling for this dataset or supply raw paired annotations and study-level extraction table in the provided text. Methodological capability must not be mistaken for evidence of missing observations.
data_or_code_leads: Appendix B is a list of 65 reviewed studies (pp. 15–16); Appendix C gives the 16-item review codebook with per-item agreement (p. 16).

COSSRAI data supplied by Xiaofei Lu (acknowledgments p. 14); data-access terms not specified. R for percent and kappa; Krippendorff and Craggs Java software for alpha, no project-specific repository or scripts identified (p. 7). No installation performed.
extraction_issues: 908 versus 236+671=907 (p. 12); leave unexplained.
Review-reporting denominator discrepancy 27 versus 28 (pp. 8 and 11); leave unresolved.
Fig. 1/6–9 curve values are not adequately extracted from supplied text; do not fabricate graph coordinates.
papers.practical_takeaway: Define shared units and multilabel agreement explicitly; separately evaluate boundaries, targets, positive agreement and semantic usefulness.

strategy_and_audit: Separate records, excluded from primary-paper and replication counts

overlap_groups.reason: Shared historical headline-test archive; subsets and pair/bundle construction differ. Not independent corpus replications.

reporting_caution_record: reviews/independent-audit.md; selected source reporting tensions, distinct from missing page locators
